statement: The square on an apotome applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a first apotome.
heath_proof: Let AB be an apotome, and CD rational, and to CD let there be applied CE equal to the square on AB and producing CF as breadth; I say that CF is a first apotome. For let BG be the annex to AB; therefore AG, GB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. [X. 73] To CD let there be applied CH equal to the square on AG, and KL equal to the square on BG. Therefore the whole CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB, and, in these, CE is equal to the square on AB; therefore the remainder FL is equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB. [II. 7] Let FM be bisected at the point N, and let NO be drawn through N parallel to CD; therefore each of the rectangles FO, LN is equal to the rectangle AG, GB. Now, since the squares on AG, GB are rational, and DM is equal to the squares on AG, GB,. therefore DM is rational. And it has been applied to the rational straight line CD, producing CM as breadth; therefore CM is rational and commensurable in length with CD. [X. 20] Again, since twice the rectangle AG, GB is medial, and FL is equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB, therefore FL is medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line CD, producing FM as breadth; therefore FM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD. [X. 22] And, since the squares on AG, GB are rational, while twice the rectangle AG, GB is medial, therefore the squares on AG, GB are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AG, GB. And CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB, and FL to twice the rectangle AG, GB; therefore DM is incommensurable with FL. But, as DM is to FL, so is CM to FM; [VI. 1] therefore CM is incommensurable in length with FM. [X. 11] And both are rational; therefore CM, MF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore CF is an apotome. [X. 73] I say next that it is also a first apotome. For, since the rectangle AG, GB is a mean proportional between the squares on AG, GB, and CH is equal to the square on AG, KL equal to the square on BG, and NL equal to the rectangle AG, GB, therefore NL is also a mean proportional between CH, KL; therefore, as CH is to NL, so is NL to KL. But, as CH is to NL, so is CK to NM, and, as NL is to KL, so is NM to KM; [VI. 1] therefore the rectangle CK, KM is equal to the square on NM [VI. 17], that is, to the fourth part of the square on FM. And, since the square on AG is commensurable with the square on GB, CH is also commensurable with KL. But, as CH is to KL, so is CK to KM; [VI. 1] therefore CK is commensurable with KM. [X. 11] Since then CM, MF are two unequal straight lines, and to CM there has been applied the rectangle CK, KM equal to the fourth part of the square on FM and deficient by a square figure, while CK is commensurable with KM, therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on MF by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CM. [X. 17] And CM is commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD set out; therefore CF is a first apotome. [X. Deff. III. 1]
ai_proof_text:
10.97
**Statement:** The square on an apotome applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a first apotome.

**Step 1.** Let AB be an apotome and CD a rational straight line. To CD apply the rectangle CE equal to the square on AB, producing CF as breadth [1.44, 1.45]. We must show that CF is a first apotome.

**Step 2.** Let BG be the annex to AB, so that AG is the whole straight line from which BG was subtracted to leave AB. Since AB is an apotome, AG and GB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.73].

**Step 3.** To CD apply the rectangle CH equal to the square on AG, producing CK as breadth, and adjoining it apply the rectangle KL equal to the square on GB, producing KM as breadth [1.44, 1.45], so that the whole CL is one rectangle applied to CD with breadth CM, and CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB together.

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AG is cut at B, the squares on AG, GB together are equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Hence CL is equal to CE together with twice the rectangle AG, GB. Therefore CL is greater than CE [CN5], so that CF is less than CM and F falls between C and M; and, subtracting CE from CL, the remainder FL is equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB [CN3].

**Step 5.** Bisect FM at N [1.10] and through N draw NO parallel to CD [1.31], meeting DL at O. The parallelograms FO and NL stand on the equal bases FN, NM and lie between the same parallels FM, EL; therefore FO is equal to NL [1.36]. Since FO and NL together make up FL, which is twice the rectangle AG, GB, each of FO, NL is equal to the rectangle AG, GB.

**Step 6.** Since AG and GB are rational, each is commensurable with the assigned rational straight line, so the squares on them are commensurable with the rational square and are rational areas [D10.1.3, D10.1.4]. Moreover, since AG, GB are commensurable in square, the squares on them are measured by the same area and so are commensurable with one another [D10.1.2, D10.1.1]. Hence the sum of the squares on AG, GB is commensurable with the square on AG [10.15], and therefore with the rational square [10.12]; that is, CL is a rational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 7.** The rational area CL is applied to the rational straight line CD, producing CM as breadth; therefore CM is rational and commensurable in length with CD [10.20].

**Step 8.** Since AG, GB are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the rectangle AG, GB is irrational and the side of the square equal to it is medial [10.21]; thus the rectangle AG, GB is a medial area, incommensurable with the rational square [D10.1.4]. Twice the rectangle AG, GB is measured by the rectangle AG, GB, so the two are commensurable [D10.1.1]; hence FL, being twice the rectangle AG, GB, is an area commensurable with a medial area and is therefore itself medial, that is, equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.23]. Further, FL, being commensurable with the rectangle AG, GB, which is incommensurable with the rational square, is itself incommensurable with the rational square [10.13].

**Step 9.** FL, equal to the square on a medial straight line, is applied to the rational straight line CD, producing FM as breadth; therefore FM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD [10.22].

**Step 10.** CL is commensurable with the rational square (Step 6), while FL is incommensurable with it (Step 8); therefore CL is incommensurable with FL [10.13]. But CL and FL are rectangles of the same height, namely CD, so CL is to FL as CM is to FM [6.1]. Therefore CM is incommensurable in length with FM [10.11].

**Step 11.** CM and MF are both rational (Steps 7 and 9), so the squares on them are rational areas, each commensurable with the rational square [D10.1.4]; hence the squares on CM, MF are commensurable with one another [10.12], that is, CM, MF are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Since they are incommensurable in length (Step 10), CM, MF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore CF, the remainder when MF is subtracted from CM, is an apotome, with whole CM and annex MF [10.73].

**Step 12.** It remains to show that CF is a first apotome. Since the square on AG and the rectangle AG, GB have the common side AG, the square on AG is to the rectangle AG, GB as AG is to GB [6.1]; likewise the rectangle AG, GB is to the square on GB as AG is to GB [6.1]. Therefore the square on AG is to the rectangle AG, GB as the rectangle AG, GB is to the square on GB [5.11]. Now CH is equal to the square on AG, NL to the rectangle AG, GB, and KL to the square on GB, and equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude [5.7]; therefore CH is to NL as NL is to KL. But CH is to NL as CK is to NM, and NL is to KL as NM is to KM [6.1]; therefore CK is to NM as NM is to KM [5.11], so that the rectangle CK, KM is equal to the square on NM [6.17].

**Step 13.** Since FM is bisected at N, the square on FM is equal to the squares on FN, NM together with twice the rectangle FN, NM [2.4], and since FN is equal to NM this is four times the square on NM. Hence the rectangle CK, KM, being equal to the square on NM, is the fourth part of the square on FM.

**Step 14.** Since the squares on AG, GB are commensurable with one another (Step 6), CH is commensurable with KL; and CH is to KL as CK is to KM [6.1]; therefore CK is commensurable in length with KM [10.11].

**Step 15.** Now CM and FM are two unequal straight lines, FM being a part of CM and therefore the less [CN5]. To the greater, CM, there has been applied the rectangle CK, KM, equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, FM, and deficient by the square on KM, and it divides CM into the parts CK, KM, which are commensurable in length. Therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on FM by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CM [10.17].

**Step 16.** Thus CF is an apotome whose whole CM is commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD set out (Step 7), and the square on the whole CM is greater than the square on the annex MF by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with CM (Step 15). Therefore CF is a first apotome [D10.3.1]. Hence the square on an apotome applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a first apotome. Q.E.D.
